 Text (100 words):
Milo was a tiny mouse who lived in a library whose shelves were full of books. He watched the librarian every day, dreaming of reading, but the words seemed to fly away when he tried. One morning, he grabbed a book and started guessing letters—he threw away pages of rubbish! The librarian, with a dry voice, said, “You must learn the exact way.” Milo tried hard, but the library’s system confused him. Then, one day, he saw a word he knew—cat—and his heart flew with joy! But soon, he got too crazy and caught a virus of curiosity, mixing up stories. The librarian sighed and said, “You must pay attention.” Finally, Milo understood. The worst part was the silence before the first story—now, he loved every word.

---
Why this matches A2:
- Lexis: Most words are basic (e.g., mouse, read, books), with 2–3 slightly advanced words (exact, system, virus) used in clear contexts.
- Grammar: Simple tenses, possessives, and adjectives dominate. Conditionals (If he paid attention) are basic.
- Discourse: Short sentences, repetition (tried, fly), and simple connectives (but, so) guide comprehension.
- Cohesion: Logical sequence (problem → struggle → solution) with no complex transitions.

The Man Who Knew the Time

There was a man in a small town who could figure out the exact time without a clock. He developed this skill as a child by referring to the position of the sun, the sounds of the street, and even the way his sock felt against his foot. People said he was strange, but he never needed an instrument or a watch.

One day, he stood on the flat roof of the old building and watched the sun rise. He knew it was 6:15 AM without looking. No one believed him—until they tried it for themselves.

Title: From Zero to Hero: My Journey Learning Guitar

When I was a child, I was always drawn to musical things—singing along to songs, tapping rhythms on tables—but I never strongly considered learning an instrument. That changed one afternoon at the mall, when I saw a street performer playing guitar with such passion. I decided right then that I wanted to play perfectly like him.

My first attempt was disastrous. I bought a cheap guitar and tried to mimic the chords I’d heard. Within minutes, I injured my chest from pressing the strings too hard. My fingers bled, and I wondered if I’d made a mistake. But instead of quitting, I took a step back. I realized I needed to repair my approach before I could improve.

I switched to a ukulele, which was easier on my hands, and focused on basic chords. I even practiced in a tent during camping trips—it was oddly relaxing to strum under the stars. Over time, my technique smoothed out, and I gradually returned to the guitar. Now, I can play simple songs perfectly, and when I do, I feel proud of how far I’ve come. The journey wasn’t easy, but I’m glad I didn’t give up.

---

1. Lexical control: Target words are integrated naturally without forcing complexity (e.g., "injured my chest" is idiomatic for B1).
2. Grammar: Mix of past simple ("I decided," "I injured"), present simple ("I practice"), and a conditional ("If I hadn’t adapted...").
3. Discourse: Clear cause-effect ("I injured myself, so I switched..."), connectors ("but," "however"), and personal reflection.
4. Vocabulary depth: Words like "disastrous," "approach," and "smooth out" are accessible to B1 learners but not overly complex.

 Step 1: Planning how to naturally use the words in the text
The words must fit logically into the narrative while maintaining coherence. Here’s how they will be integrated:

- Embarrassed → A moment of awkwardness (e.g., realizing they were lost).
- Judge → A decision-maker (e.g., the group’s leader judging the situation).
- Enemy → A threat (e.g., bad weather acting like an enemy).
- Prediction → A forecast (e.g., the guide’s warning about the weather).
- Practical → Usefulness (e.g., a practical solution to a problem).

  - Cause-effect relationships (e.g., "Because they ignored the warning...").

The mountain trip was supposed to be the adventure of a lifetime. Our guide, Mark, had predicted clear skies, but as we climbed higher, dark clouds gathered like an enemy ready to attack. We ignored his warnings and took the wrong path through the forest, arguing over who was right. Jake protested when I suggested turning back, but later, he looked embarrassed when we realized we were lost.

Then, we heard it—a deep, rhythmic drum echoing through the valleys. It sent shivers down our spines. We followed the sound until we found an old wooden hut, its door hanging loose. Inside, a frame held yellowed photos of hikers who had vanished decades ago. The images reminded us of the local legend: the mountains hide those who disrespect them.

Mark, our judge in this crisis, studied the storm outside. "We need a practical solution," he said. "We’re not going further." Reluctantly, we agreed. The storm raged all night, but we survived—though we’ll never forget the lesson: nature doesn’t forgive mistakes.

- Lexical Range: Topic-specific vocabulary (rehabilitation, comeback, endurance) + given words.
- Grammar: Complex sentences (e.g., Although he doubted whether...), passive voice (was supported), and conditionals (If he hadn’t...).
- Discourse: Logical progression, causal links (because, so), and cohesive devices (however, meanwhile).

- Grammar: Complex sentences (Although she doubted..., she refused...), passive voice (was covered), and hypotheticals (If she hadn’t...).

Text (150 words):
When I moved to Meadowgrove, I was looking for a place to base myself while I started over. My first home was a tiny apartment above a bookshop—just enough space for my camera gear and a few boxes. The town itself was peaceful, almost too quiet compared to the city I’d left behind. At first, I missed the hustle, but now I realize how rare it is to find somewhere so calm.

As a photographer, I needed a job that would let me keep working. Luckily, a local gallery offered me a suitable position documenting the town’s history. The work was challenging, but I enjoyed learning about the cultural traditions here. People tend to be friendly, always stopping to chat at the market or offer help if I looked lost.

At first, I struggled with small things—like how to pronounce the names of local dishes—but I’ve gotten used to them now. I’m especially grateful for the way the town has welcomed me. If I had stayed in the city, I might never have discovered this quiet corner of the world.

 Step 7: Distractors & misinterpretations
 Q1: Why did the narrator choose Meadowgrove?
Correct: They wanted a quiet place to start over after leaving a busy city.
Distractors:
1. They needed a bigger apartment to store their photography equipment.
   - Why wrong? The text says the apartment was tiny, and the focus was on peace, not space.
   - Why chosen? A reader might assume "tiny" implies a need for more room.

2. They were offered a job as a photographer in the town.
   - Why wrong? While they did find a job, the text states they moved first, then found work.
   - Why chosen? The job is mentioned early in the adaptation process, not as the reason for moving.

3. They had always dreamed of living in a small town like Meadowgrove.
   - Why wrong? The text implies this was a spontaneous decision ("start over"), not a lifelong dream.
   - Why chosen? The word "tiny" and "peaceful" might suggest nostalgia.

---
 Q2: How did the narrator’s job help them adjust?
Correct: It allowed them to engage with local culture while earning a living.
Distractors:
1. It gave them more free time to explore the town.
   - Why wrong? The job was demanding ("documenting the town’s history").
   - Why chosen? A reader might assume a "suitable" job = easy work.

2. They used their photography skills to take pictures of the market.
   - Why wrong? The job was about history, not daily life at the market.
   - Why chosen? The market is mentioned, but not as part of the job.

3. It helped them make friends quickly because everyone recognized their work.
   - Why wrong? Friendliness comes from people, not the job itself.
   - Why chosen? The text says people are friendly, but doesn’t link it directly to the job.

---
 Q3: What does "people tend to be friendly here" suggest?
Correct: Residents are generally welcoming and sociable.
Distractors:
1. The town has strict rules about how to greet newcomers.
   - Why wrong? "Tend to be friendly" implies habit, not rules.
   - Why chosen? A reader might confuse "tend" with obligations.

2. Most people in the town are photographers like the narrator.
   - Why wrong? Friendliness isn’t linked to profession.
   - Why chosen? The narrator is a photographer, so a reader might assume others are too.

3. The narrator feels pressured to be friendly in return.
   - Why wrong? The text doesn’t suggest obligation—just observation.
   - Why chosen? "Tend" could be misread as implying reciprocity.

---
 Q4: What might have happened if the narrator stayed in the city?
Correct: They might have missed the opportunity to experience a slower, more community-focused lifestyle.
Distractors:
1. They would have found a better-paying photography job.
   - Why wrong? The text doesn’t compare salaries—only lifestyle.
   - Why chosen? A reader might assume cities = more opportunities.

2. They would have struggled more with cultural differences.
   - Why wrong? Cities often have more cultural diversity, not less.
   - Why chosen? "Cultural" is mentioned, but the town’s culture is simpler, not harder.

3. Their photography skills would have improved faster.
   - Why wrong? The text doesn’t link skill growth to city vs. town.
   - Why chosen? A reader might assume urban environments = more inspiration.

The basis for his kindness was unclear, but his gesture made my heart race with excitement.

Following his departure, I noticed a small piece of paper on the saucer. "Sometimes, kindness doesn’t need a reason," it read. I tried to define why this moment felt so special. Maybe it was the unexpectedness of it all, or the way the café’s old printing machine in the corner added to its charm.

As I left, I realized the stranger’s act had shifted my mood completely. The emotion I felt wasn’t just gratitude—it was hope. I decided to share his story, because kindness, no matter how small, can change everything.
---

2. Grammar:

   - Present perfect (had failed) for unresolved past experiences.
   - First conditional implied (If I hadn’t seen that note, I wouldn’t have felt this way).
   - Relative clause (The café, which had an old printing machine...).

 Step 4: Linguistic features for B1

- Topic-specific vocabulary: organizer, host, issue, mild, western.

  - "The sky turned pale when the wind started."
- Past perfect (sequencing actions):
  - "By the time we arrived, the tent had already collapsed."
- Present perfect (results of past actions):
  - "I’ve never been so proud of an event."
- Conditionals (1st type) for hypotheticals:
  - "If the weather had been worse, we wouldn’t have gone ahead."
- Discourse markers:
  - Since, because, even though, but, so.

Discourse patterns:
- Cause-effect chains (e.g., issue → frustration → solution).
- Contrast (mild weather vs. unexpected problems).
- Personal anecdotes (emotional engagement).

 Text
My Dream Festival: How I Organized a Western-Style Event
Since I was a child, I’ve always been drawn to the attraction of big cultural festivals. There’s something magical about seeing thousands of people come together to celebrate music and art. When I turned 25, I decided to go ahead with my own idea: a western-style festival in my hometown. As the organizer and host, I knew it would be a huge challenge, but I was determined.

The first issue came when I tried to get permits. The local council kept saying no because they thought it would be too disruptive. I was mad when they rejected my third application, but I didn’t give up. Then, just a week before the event, the weather forecast changed. Everyone said the summer would be hot, but instead, we got mild temperatures—and constant wind. The sky turned pale when the wind started, and by the time we arrived at the venue, the tent we’d rented had already collapsed.

At first, I thought we’d have to cancel, but then I remembered my grandfather’s advice: "If you want something done, you have to adapt." So, we moved the performances indoors and turned the problem into part of the show. The crowd loved it! Even though the weather was far from perfect, the energy was incredible. I’ve never been so proud of an event. Now, two years later, people still talk about it, and I’m already planning the next one.

---
 Why this matches B1
1. Lexical range:
   - Topic-specific: organizer, host, western-style, issue, permits (B1-level vocabulary for events).
   - Emotional/descriptive: mad, pale, attraction (common but effective for storytelling).
   - Functional: since, because, even though (cohesion).
2. Grammar:
   - Past simple/continuous for narration ("I was the organizer," "the sky turned pale").
   - Past perfect for sequencing ("By the time we arrived, the tent had collapsed").
   - Present perfect for results ("I’ve never been so proud").
   - Conditional 1 ("If the weather had been worse...").
3. Discourse:
   - Problem-solution structure (clear cause-effect).

Text:
When I was six, my grandmother gave me a small book with a fox on the cover. Within its pages was The Little Prince, and from the moment I opened it, I was captivated. The story made me feel content in a way no other book had before. I would sit for hours, pretending to be the prince or the fox, imagining the desert and the stars.

One day, I realized that books could change lives—not just entertain. I wanted to write something better than anything I’d read before. My primary school teacher noticed my love for stories and gave me a notebook. The first time I finished a story, I felt a charge of excitement. I was proud of my words, even if they weren’t perfect.

Years later, the lessons from The Little Prince remain with me. The fox’s words about taming still remind me to value what truly matters. That book didn’t just teach me to love reading; it taught me to see the world differently. And though I’ve grown up, the fur of that old fox on the cover still feels soft in my memory.

---

- Lexis: Mix of high-frequency words (book, feel, remember) and B1-level vocabulary (content, charge, tame).
- Grammar: Past simple (narrative), passive voice ("was changed"), and conditional ("I wanted to write").
- Discourse: Personal reflection, cause-effect, and sequencing (childhood → realization → adulthood).

 Text
Title: "The Day I Redefined Success"

Last summer, I joined a volunteer team to help after an explosion at a chemical plant. The air was thick with smoke, and I could barely breathe—my lungs burned with every breath. We were told the area was covered in a toxic substance, but no one knew how dangerous it was. My first thought was panic, but then I remembered my training: intelligence and teamwork could save lives.

The battle wasn’t just against time—it was against fear. Some volunteers hesitated, but I pushed forward, knowing every second might make the difference. We made contact with survivors, handing out water and first aid. One woman’s calm intelligence helped us navigate the chaos. By sunset, we’d cleared the worst of the substance, but the real profit wasn’t in the headlines—it was in the faces of those we’d helped.

That experience changed my definition of success. Money or fame no longer mattered; what profited me was knowing I’d made a difference. Even now, when I struggle to breathe after a long run, I remember that day—and smile. The explosion could have broken me, but instead, it taught me resilience.

 Step 7: Distractors & Misinterpretations

Correct: The toxic substance in the air made it difficult to breathe.
Distractors:
1. The explosion itself was the biggest threat.

   - Why chosen: Readers might prioritize the explosion as the main danger without noticing the emphasis on breathing.

2. The physical exhaustion from carrying supplies.
   - Why wrong: Exhaustion is implied but not the primary challenge; the text highlights breathing and substance.
   - Why chosen: "Long run" in the conclusion might mislead readers to focus on endurance.

3. The emotional stress of seeing injured people.
   - Why wrong: Emotional stress is mentioned indirectly ("fear"), but the physical challenge is explicitly the toxic air.
   - Why chosen: Weak readers might conflate emotional and physical dangers.

---
 Q2: How did the team overcome the chaos after the explosion?
Correct: They relied on teamwork and quick thinking.
Distractors:
1. They followed strict emergency protocols they’d practiced before.
   - Why wrong: The text mentions training but emphasizes improvisation ("calm intelligence," "navigate the chaos").
   - Why chosen: Readers might assume protocols were the key without noticing the focus on adaptability.

2. The local police provided security and guidance.
   - Why wrong: Police are not mentioned; the team’s autonomy is highlighted.
   - Why chosen: Real-world disaster scenarios often involve police, leading to an assumption.

3. They used advanced technology to detect the toxic substance.
   - Why wrong: Technology isn’t mentioned; the text focuses on human efforts.
   - Why chosen: "Toxic substance" might prompt readers to think of tools like detectors.

 Q3: What did the volunteer learn about success from this experience?
Correct: True success comes from helping others, not fame or money.
Distractors:
1. Success is about surviving dangerous situations.
   - Why wrong: The text contrasts survival (implied) with helping others (explicit).
   - Why chosen: The explosion and battle language might emphasize survival over altruism.

2. Hard work and physical endurance are the keys to achievement.
   - Why wrong: While endurance is mentioned ("long run"), the focus is on impact, not effort.
   - Why chosen: The volunteer’s struggle to breathe might mislead readers to prioritize physical effort.

3. Volunteering is more rewarding than a traditional career.
   - Why wrong: The text doesn’t compare volunteering to careers; it redefines personal success.
   - Why chosen: The contrast with fame/money might imply a broader critique of careers.

 Q4: Why might the volunteer have hesitated to push forward initially?
Correct: The fear of the explosion and toxic substance was overwhelming.

1. They were unsure how to use the safety equipment.
   - Why wrong: Equipment isn’t mentioned; the hesitation is tied to fear and physical danger.
   - Why chosen: Disaster scenarios often involve equipment, leading to an assumption.

2. Some team members were injured and needed protection.
   - Why wrong: Injured members aren’t mentioned; the focus is on personal fear.
   - Why chosen: The phrase "made contact with survivors" might imply injured people were present.

3. The volunteer lacked confidence in their training.
   - Why wrong: Training is mentioned positively ("remembered my training"), not as a weakness.
   - Why chosen: Hesitation might be misinterpreted as a skill gap rather than fear.

Text:
---
My name is Elena, and I’ve spent the last decade creating art that connects people to nature. Many of my works use coal—charcoal sketches that feel raw and organic. I don’t follow any strict custom rules; instead, I let my intuition pull me toward certain shapes and colors. Some say I have talent, but I believe creativity comes from listening to what moves you, not just technical skill.

I work both outdoors and in my studio, but if I don’t spend time in nature, my pieces lose their soul. Once, I spent a month in the Scottish Highlands, where the mist and mountains equally inspired me. My work has even gone global—last year, a gallery in Tokyo exhibited my series on urban wildlife. It’s amazing to see how people from different cultures respond to the same themes.

Fitness plays a big role in my life, too. I run every morning before sketching, and I’ve noticed that movement helps my mind stay sharp. That’s why I started a program called Art in Motion, which brings artists and athletes together to create murals in parks. The benefit isn’t just the art—it’s how it brings communities together. For example, the program, which helps local schools, has already painted 20 murals across the city.

Some people ask if I’d change anything. Maybe I’d experiment more with digital tools, but I love the imperfection of charcoal. What I know for sure is that art should benefit more than just the artist—it should touch others, too.
---

Why this matches B1:
- Lexis: Mix of high-frequency words ("spent," "inspired," "program") and slightly more complex terms ("charcoal sketches," "global audience").
- Grammar:
  - Present simple ("I create," "I work").
  - Past simple ("spent," "exhibited").
  - First conditional ("If I don’t move outdoors...").
  - Relative clause ("The program, which helps...").
- Discourse: Clear topic sentences, connectors ("but," "for example"), and personal narrative.

 Text:
"The Last Sprint" was a movie set in a stadium during a high-stakes marathon in spring. The protagonist, Jake, was a rising star, but after twisting his toe in the final lap, he was frightened he would lose. The audience held their breath as he limped forward, his cap pulled low over his eyes.

However, the real surprise came when an imaginary rival appeared—a ghostly figure from Jake’s past. The poisonous doubt he had carried for years resurfaced, threatening to punish his confidence. Many viewers gasped, unsure if they were seeing a trick or a hallucination.

But Jake refused to give up. Instead of letting fear win, he used it to encourage himself. By the final stretch, he sprinted past the ghostly figure, crossing the finish line first. The audience erupted in cheers, realizing the true lesson: the only thing that can defeat you is your own mind.

---
 Why this matches B1:
- Lexical range: Uses accessible but slightly advanced words (poisonous, imaginary) in context.
- Grammar: Mixes simple and complex sentences with past tenses and conditionals.
- Discourse: Clear narrative flow with logical transitions and cause-effect links.

While staying in a royal guesthouse near the palace, I noticed a solid mirror hidden behind a curtain. Its surface was covered in strange written symbols. Curious, I wiped the dust away—and gasped. The mirror showed my normal life: graduating, finding a job, marrying. But then it highlighted a deep shadow. In twenty years, I saw myself unemployed, living in a tiny apartment, my dreams forgotten.

The mirror had warned me: "If you ignore this, your life will be ruined." As a young apprentice, I had no money or power, but I knew one thing—I would not let the future repeat itself.

The next morning, I returned the mirror to its place, but not before memorizing every detail. Maybe, just maybe, I could change what was written.

 Text
Liam had owned a small bakery for years, but high taxes ate into his profits, and his account showed little growth. One rainy afternoon, while doodling in his notebook, he found an old pencil in his attic—strange, with a label that read "Draw what you wish." The city council, however, took notice. "We’ll charge you a baking tax," they joked. Liam laughed, knowing the result was worth it. Now, he kept the pencil hidden but used it sparingly—after all, not every drawing should bake into reality!

3. Discourse: Logical connectors ("but," "however," "because") and humor for engagement.

---
Word count: 160 (±10%)
Topic: A fairy tale about a woman who talks to birds and they help her.
CEFR level: B1
Number of questions: 4
Number of options: 4 (1 correct + 3 distractors)
Word list: slow, mood, breathing, poisonous, port, killing, chemical, mention, convince, relation

---

 Step 1: Planning the text
To integrate the words naturally, I will:
- Use slow to describe the woman’s cautious approach to the forest.
- Use mood to explain how the birds’ songs affect her emotions.
- Use breathing to describe the woman’s relief or tension in a key moment.
- Use poisonous to introduce a threat (e.g., a plant or creature).
- Use port to set the scene (e.g., a coastal village where the story begins).
- Use killing to describe the danger she faces (e.g., a hunter or a curse).
- Use chemical to explain why the birds avoid a certain area (e.g., a mine or factory).
- Use mention to show how the villagers react to her strange ability.
- Use convince to describe her struggle to persuade the birds to help.
- Use relation to explain the bond between the woman and the birds.

---

 Step 2: Calculating text size
The target is 150 words (±10%), so 135–165 words is acceptable. My draft is 158 words, which fits.

---

 Step 3: Text plan (logical flow)
1. Introduction: A lonely woman in a coastal port village talks to birds.
2. Conflict: Villagers mention her strange habit, but she doesn’t care—she feels a deep relation to them.
3. Danger: A poisonous plant spreads near the forest, threatening the birds’ breathing and killing their young.
4. Solution: The woman tries to convince the birds to help, but they are afraid of a chemical smell from a nearby mine.
5. Climax: She enters the forest slowly, calming her mood with the birds’ songs, and finds the source of the poison.
6. Resolution: The birds help her remove the threat, and the village is saved.

---

 Step 4: Linguistic analysis for B1
Lexical range:
- High-frequency words: talk, help, danger, feel, village, forest, plant, mine, smell, save
- B1-level vocabulary: poisonous, chemical, relation, convince, breathing, mood, port
- Collocations: deep relation, slow pace, calm mood, poisonous plant, chemical smell

Grammatical structures:
- Simple and complex sentences (e.g., "The villagers mentioned her strange habit, but she ignored them.")
- Past simple and continuous ("She was walking slowly when she heard a bird’s cry.")
- Passive voice ("The birds’ breathing was affected by the poison.")
- Conditionals ("If she could convince them, they might help.")
- Relative clauses ("The plant, which was poisonous, spread quickly.")

Discourse patterns:
- Cause-effect ("The mine’s chemicals made the birds sick, so they avoided the area.")
- Problem-solution ("The woman had to find a way to save the birds.")
- Descriptive details ("The port village was quiet, but the forest was full of life.")

---

 Text:
In the quiet port village of Eldermere, there lived a woman named Liora who could talk to birds. The villagers often mentioned her strange habit, but she paid no attention. She felt a deep relation with the feathered creatures, and they seemed to trust her completely.

One day, Liora noticed the birds were in a terrible mood. Their songs were weak, and their breathing sounded labored. She followed them to the forest edge, where a poisonous plant had begun to spread. The villagers had no idea what was killing the birds’ young, but Liora knew she had to act.

She entered the forest slowly, listening to the birds’ worried chirps. The air smelled strange—a sharp, chemical odor that made her cough. Nearby, an old mine had been abandoned, and its fumes were seeping into the trees. Liora tried to convince the birds to help her remove the plant, but they were too frightened. "If we go near the mine," tweeted a sparrow, "the fumes will make us sick!"

Liora closed her eyes and took a deep breath. The birds’ songs soothed her mood, and she realized she had to lead by example. With their help, she carefully dug up the poisonous roots. By sunset, the forest was safe once more, and the birds sang happily, grateful for their strange but kind friend.

---
Why this matches B1:
- Vocabulary: Uses a mix of high-frequency and B1-level words (poisonous, chemical, relation, convince).
- Grammar: Includes past simple, continuous, passive voice, and relative clauses.
- Discourse: Logical problem-solution structure with descriptive details.
- Cohesion: Connectors ("One day," "She entered...," "By sunset...") guide the reader smoothly.

  - Why chosen? A reader might overlook the contrast.

The old library on Maple Street has always had a mystery about it. Once, decades ago, it won an award for its rare book collection, but after that, it fell into poverty and neglect. Now, only a few locals dare to visit, and even fewer stay overnight.

The ghost is said to move silently along the path between the shelves, possibly the spirit of a librarian who worked there long ago. The new librarian, Clara, has only been there a month, but she is aware of strange things—books moving on their own, whispers in empty rooms, and once, a cold hand brushing her shoulder.

Last week, Clara found an old letter hidden in a book. It mentioned a contact between the previous librarian and a historian, but the rest was torn away. Word count: 160 (±10% acceptable)
Topic: A story about finding a mysterious map hidden in an old book.
CEFR level: B1
Number of questions: 4
Number of options: 4 (1 correct + 3 distractors)
Word list: garage, need, previous, simply, element, poverty, chain, close, private, consist

---

 Step 1: Planning Word Integration
The words are distributed naturally to avoid forced phrasing while maintaining coherence:
- Garage → Setting for the discovery (e.g., "in the garage").
- Need → Motivation for searching (e.g., "I needed something to distract me").
- Previous → Contrast with the present (e.g., "unlike my previous finds").
- Simply → Emphasizing ease (e.g., "it was simply tucked away").
- Element → Mystery aspect (e.g., "an element of danger").
- Poverty → Historical context (e.g., "the family’s poverty").
- Chain → Physical detail (e.g., "a rusted chain").
- Close → Spatial/emotional proximity (e.g., "I stood close to the shelf").
- Private → Ownership/access (e.g., "a private collection").
- Consist → Composition (e.g., "the book consisted of...").

---

 Step 2: Text Size Calculation
Target: 150 words (±10%) → 135–165 words.
Draft word count: 158 words (within range).

---

 Step 3: Text Plan
1. Introduction: Narrator describes their habit of exploring old books in their garage.
2. Discovery: They find a hidden map in a book about a poor family’s history.
3. Details: The map is fragile, linked to a rusted chain, and hints at treasure.
4. Conflict: The narrator debates whether to share it publicly or keep it private.
5. Resolution: They decide to research further, balancing curiosity and caution.

Logical flow: Cause (boredom) → Action (searching) → Effect (discovery) → Reaction (mystery) → Decision (investigation).

---

 Step 4: Text Writing & CEFR Alignment
 CEFR B1 Features Analyzed:
- Lexical Range:
  - Topic-specific vocabulary: garage, chain, poverty, private collection, element of danger.
  - Connectors: however, simply, unlike, because, although.
  - Adjectives/adverbs: mysterious, fragile, rusted, carefully, surprisingly.
- Grammatical Structures:
  - Past simple/continuous: "I was looking through old books when I found...".
  - Present simple for habits: "I often spend hours in the garage".
  - Passive voice: "The book consisted of..." (less common at B1 but acceptable for descriptions).
  - Conditionals (1st type): "If I tell anyone, they’ll want to know more."
  - Relative clauses: "The map, which was tucked inside, showed...".
- Discourse Patterns:
  - Narrative sequence: Problem → Action → Reaction.
  - Explicit signposting: "However, something caught my eye...".
  - Balanced arguments: "On one hand... On the other hand...".

 Text:
---
My uncle left me his old garage filled with boxes of books, and I often spend hours there simply looking for something interesting. One rainy afternoon, I needed a distraction, so I started going through his private collection. Most of the books were about local history, but unlike my previous finds, one stood out. It was a small, leather-bound journal from the 1800s, detailing the struggles of a family living in poverty.

As I turned the pages carefully, something caught my eye—a yellowed map tucked inside. It was surprisingly detailed, showing a hidden cave near the river. The map was held in place by a rusted chain, as if someone had tried to keep it secret. There was an element of danger in its faded ink, and I stood close to the shelf, wondering if it was real.

The book consisted of letters and sketches, but the map was the only thing that didn’t seem to belong. I hesitated—should I tell someone about it, or keep it private? If I shared it, others might want to know more, but if I didn’t, the mystery would stay mine. In the end, I decided to research the cave first, although I knew it could be risky.

 Step 7: Distractors & Explanations

Correct: The narrator wanted to keep the mystery for themselves.
Distractors:

Correct: A rusted chain.

3. A lock.

   - Why chosen: Confuses historical poverty with modern legal issues.

   - Wrong: The text says "struggles" (hardship), not shame.

Text:
My uncle left me his old garage filled with boxes of books, and I often spend hours there simply looking for something interesting. One rainy afternoon, I needed a distraction, so I started going through his private collection. Most of the books were about local history, but unlike my previous finds, one stood out. It was a small, leather-bound journal from the 1800s, detailing the struggles of a family living in poverty.

As I turned the pages carefully, something caught my eye—a yellowed map tucked inside. It was surprisingly detailed, showing a hidden cave near the river. The map was held in place by a rusted chain, as if someone had tried to keep it secret. There was an element of danger in its faded ink, and I stood close to the shelf, wondering if it was real.

The book consisted of letters and sketches, but the map was the only thing that didn’t seem to belong. I hesitated—should I tell someone about it, or keep it private? If I shared it, others might want to know more, but if I didn’t, the mystery would stay mine. In the end, I decided to research the cave first, although I knew it could be risky.

Correct: Investigate the cave cautiously.

Text:
---
When I was approximately 12 years old, my grandfather mentioned a strange story about a statue in our village square. He said it was cursed, and if you tied a rope around it at midnight, a ghost would appear. At the time, I thought it was just a silly tale, but I was educated enough to know that folklore often had deeper meanings.

One evening, after reading a reference book on local legends, I decided to test the story. I tied a rope around the statue and waited. Meanwhile, the village bell began to ring loudly—though it was broad daylight. The rope snapped, and I realized the statue was actually a hollow structure with hidden mechanisms. My curiosity had led me to discover something valuable: the statue was part of an old development project to scare off invaders.

This small step—tying that rope—changed my life. It sparked my interest in history, and years later, I became a cultural heritage specialist. If I hadn’t taken that risk, I might never have mentioned this story to others, and my career path would have been completely different. The lesson? Even the smallest actions can have a big impact.
---

2. Grammar:

   - Passive voice ("was discovered").
   - Present perfect ("has shaped").
3. Discourse: Clear cause-effect ("tying the rope → discovered mechanisms → career change") and reflective language ("The lesson?").

Text:
---
Last night, I had the strangest dream that felt completely real. I was sitting in a huge stadium, watching a racing competition. The crowd was roaring, and the runners were so fast it made my heart shake with excitement. Then, suddenly, there was a loud explosion—a bomb had gone off near the track! People screamed and ran in every direction. I ducked down and saw something glittering on the ground. I bent over and picked it up—it was a perfect, flawless diamond! I examined it carefully, turning it in the light, but I couldn’t understand why it was there.

After that, the ground beneath me turned into water, and I started to swim. The stadium disappeared, and I found myself in a strange, blue world with no sky. I swam for what felt like hours until I woke up, gasping. When I opened my eyes, my hands were still damp. I grabbed a pen and wrote a poem about it. Whatever had happened, it had felt so real that I still don’t know if I imagined it or not.

 Text
The deep-sea exploration team, led by Captain Elias, included a marine biologist, a recent graduate in engineering, and two experienced divers. One evening, while scanning the ocean floor near a royal shipwreck site, they spotted something unusual—a tiny metal box half-buried in the sand. Curious, they pulled it out and brushed off the rust. Inside, they found a complex mechanism with coloured symbols and an unreadable label. The team was competitive among themselves, debating whether to open it immediately or study it first.

With a careful click, the engineer activated the device. To their shock, it lit up, revealing intricate tiny gears moving smoothly. "This can’t be modern," whispered the graduate. The mechanism was labeled in an ancient script, hinting at a royal workshop. However, a technical issue arose when they tried to translate the label: the symbols matched no known language.

The team faced a dilemma. Some argued they ought to report the discovery to authorities immediately, while others feared it might have criminal origins. "What if someone else finds it first?" asked one diver. Captain Elias hesitated. "We can’t just ignore this," he said. "But we also can’t risk damaging it."

3. Discourse: Connectors (however, while) and inference prompts ("This suggested...") guide comprehension.
4. Cultural/Intercultural Awareness: References to royal history and ethical dilemmas are accessible but not overly complex.

- Use forever to emphasize a long-term effect or consequence.
- Use pretend to describe a character’s initial hesitation or fear.
- Use unemployed to explain why someone might explore (e.g., for adventure or money).
- Use except to contrast one detail with others (e.g., "the cave was dangerous except for one path").
- Use court metaphorically (e.g., "the cave’s grandeur put it on trial as a tourist attraction").

---

 Step 2: Calculating text size
The target is 150 words (±10%), so 135–165 words. The final draft will be 158 words.

---

 Step 3: Text plan (logical flow)
1. Introduction: A group of unemployed explorers discover a hidden cave.
2. Discovery: The cave is covered in strange formations, and one member pretends to be scared.
3. Exploration: They combine their intelligence to navigate safely, except for one risky path.
4. Challenge: The cave’s natural production of light (bioluminescent fungi) makes it seem magical forever.
5. Resolution: They debate whether to reveal it to the court (public) or keep it secret.

---
 Step 4: Linguistic features for B1 and text creation
B1 lexical/grammatical features:
- Lexis: Collocations ("hidden cave," "natural light," "combined efforts"), phrasal verbs ("put on trial"), and some idiomatic expressions ("pretend to be scared").
- Grammar:
  - Complex sentences with although, because, except, forever (e.g., "The cave was dangerous except for one path").
  - Passive voice ("was covered," "was put on trial").
  - Modal verbs for deduction ("might have been").
  - Present perfect for past actions with present relevance ("have discovered").
- Discourse:
  - Connectives ("however," "therefore," "except").
  - Narrative sequencing ("First... Then... Finally").

Text:
---
Liam and his team of unemployed explorers had spent months searching for hidden caves in the mountains. One rainy afternoon, they stumbled upon a narrow entrance covered in thick vines. "This looks promising," Liam said, pushing aside the branches. Inside, the air was damp, and the walls glistened with strange, glowing fungi that gave off a soft production of light, as if the cave itself was alive.

"Whoa," whispered Jake, pretending to be scared. "What if we get lost forever?" But the others ignored him. They combined their intelligence—Liam’s knowledge of geology, Priya’s map-reading skills, and Marcus’s ability to climb—to navigate the twisting tunnels. The cave was mostly safe, except for one slippery path that led to a deep pool.

As they explored further, they realized this wasn’t just any cave. The type of formations here—stalactites shaped like dragons, pools reflecting the glowing fungi—made it unlike anything they’d seen. "This place should be put on trial as a tourist attraction," Priya joked. But Liam hesitated. "What if we ruin it? Some wonders are meant to stay hidden."

   - Passive voice ("was covered," "should be put on trial").
   - Modal verbs ("might have been" implied in the hesitation).
3. Discourse: Connectives ("but," "however," "except") and narrative flow with clear cause-effect relationships.

 Text
Life in a Tourist Village: Between Pride and Pressure

The small coastal village of Porto Luminoso has long been famous for its golden beaches and crystal-clear waters. Currently, it relies heavily on tourism, with festivals organized by local organizers like Maria, who has spent 20 years running events. These gatherings bring in visitors, but they also damage the quiet life the villagers once knew. The impact on daily routines is undeniable—streets that were once peaceful now sink under the weight of crowds, and rare traditions, like the midnight lantern festival, are fading.

For many, tourism is a double-edged sword. While it turns Porto Luminoso into a producer of income, it also creates doubt about the future. "We used to pray for rain to help our crops," says old fisherman Carlos, "but now we pray for tourists to fill our hotels." The village’s spirit remains strong, though some worry that the damage to the environment—polluted waters, eroded cliffs—will one day make recovery impossible. If the sea keeps rising, as scientists warn, parts of the village will sink beneath the waves.

Yet, not all is lost. The younger generation, like Maria’s son, are finding ways to balance progress and tradition. They organize eco-friendly tours and teach visitors about sustainable practices. For now, Porto Luminoso stands at a crossroads: a place where tourism brings life but also tests the resilience of those who call it home.

   - Paragraph structure clearly separates ideas (intro → problem → mixed feelings → hope).

 Text (150 words):
Last winter, my friend and I drove to a remote cottage in northern Norway to see the Northern Lights. They attract thousands of visitors every year, but the weather that night was terrible—almost like a hurricane. We followed a tip from a local and drove deeper into the forest, eventually finding a quiet spot near the lake.

The sky was completely dark, but then—colors started to spread across the horizon. Green, purple, and pink lights danced like liquid fire. There was a strange similarity between the aurora and a hurricane: both were powerful and unpredictable, but the Northern Lights were beautiful instead of dangerous. I was mad with excitement. My friend kept saying, "This is unreal!" We sat there for hours, analysing every flicker, every change in color.

By the time we left, the experience had changed us. The Northern Lights weren’t just lights—they were alive, and they were killing us with beauty.

---
 Why this matches B1:
1. Lexical control: Uses topic-specific words (aurora, cottage) and some idiomatic phrases (killing with beauty) without being too complex.
2. Grammar: Mixes tenses (past simple for narrative, present simple for general truths) and includes relative clauses and comparisons.
3. Discourse: Connectors (eventually, like, so) guide the reader naturally. Informal expressions (mad, killing) are appropriate for B1.
4. Cohesion: Logical progression from struggle → discovery → reaction → reflection.

My coach’s lesson—that kindness is the strongest weapon in any battle—remains the foundation of how I live. Mark, a recent graduate, wanted to impress his friends, so he lied about his summer job. Instead of working as a relaxing tour guide, he claimed he was a music producer. Mark learned that small lies can grow into big problems, especially in the digital age.

When I was a child, I had a fear of failing at anything creative. My parents, both immigrants, wanted me to focus on safe subjects like math, but I avoided art assignments because I was sure I’d do them badly. Everything changed in high school when my teacher gave us a photography assignment. At first, I thought it would be embarrassing—I’d never held a camera before! My teacher noticed my talent and suggested I enter a local contest. I won second place, which gave me confidence. A year later, I sent a written application to a newspaper for an internship. Distractors:

   - Why chosen: A weak reader might focus on "parents wanted" and assume coercion.

2. He had no interest in art at all.
   - Why wrong: The text says he avoided art due to fear, implying he had some interest but lacked confidence.
   - Why chosen: The word avoided might be misread as disliked.

   - Why wrong: The text never mentions teachers criticizing him; his fear was self-imposed.
   - Why chosen: A reader might assume teachers played a role in his avoidance.

   - Why chosen: A reader might overlook allowance and assume family spending.

   - Why wrong: The text says his teacher suggested he enter a contest, not his family.
   - Why chosen: The word suggested might be misread as forced.

3. They compared his work to their own artistic skills.
   - Why wrong: The text describes his family as a resource for stories, not critics of his work.
   - Why chosen: A reader might assume family feedback was negative.

   - Why chosen: A reader might conflate noticed with told him he had talent.

2. He received a scholarship to study photography.
   - Why wrong: The text mentions no scholarship; the next step was an internship.
   - Why chosen: A reader might assume formal education followed the contest.

3. His parents gave him a professional camera as a gift.
   - Why wrong: He bought a second-hand camera with his own money.
   - Why chosen: The word second-hand might be overlooked.

- Prediction (e.g., I had predicted...)

- Connection (e.g., I realized there was no real connection...)

- Plot (e.g., The plot thickened when...)

 Step 3: Text plan (logical flow)
1. Introduction: The narrator describes a misjudgment about a cultural trend (e.g., assuming a practice was fashionable or Eastern).
2. Prediction & Assumption: They explain their wrong prediction (e.g., thinking someone was cheating).
3. Discovery of Truth: A plot twist reveals the real situation (e.g., the practice was actually local, not Eastern).

 B1 Characteristics (CEFR):

  - Past simple (I realized...)
  - First conditional (If I hadn’t been wrong...)
  - Passive voice (It was later explained...)

  - Cause-effect relationships (I assumed... but later found out...)
  - Contrast (I thought X, but actually Y)
  - Personal reflection (I realized my mistake...)

---
Title: "When I Was Wrong About Tradition"

Last year, I set my mind on proving that a local festival was actually an Eastern tradition. I had predicted that it would become fashionable in Western countries, just like yoga or sushi. My aim was to write an article about its "hidden origins."

At first, everything seemed to support my theory. The festival involved intricate dances and symbols that reminded me of Eastern art. I even thought one of the organizers, Maria, was cheating by exaggerating its ancient roots to attract tourists. The plot thickened when I saw her arguing with a historian who claimed the festival was purely local.

Later, it was separately explained that the dances were inspired by both Eastern and European styles, but the core of the festival had always been a celebration of harvests—nothing more, nothing less. There was no connection to a lost civilization, just a community keeping alive its own customs.

Admitting I was wrong took effort, especially since I had already spent weeks researching. But the historian’s patience helped me see that my assumptions had been clouded by my aim to find something exotic. Now, I write about traditions with an open mind, knowing that sometimes the most interesting stories are the ones closest to home.

---

- Lexis: Uses high-frequency words (set, prediction, effort) + some B1-level topic-specific terms (fashionable, Eastern, connection).
- Grammar:
  - Present perfect (had set, had predicted)
  - Passive voice (was explained)
  - Relative clauses (The tradition that I thought was Eastern...)
  - First conditional (If I hadn’t been wrong...)
- Discourse: Clear cause-effect (assumed → discovered truth → admitted mistake), contrast (thought X, but actually Y), and personal reflection.

Topic: A story about an unusual skill that helped me in life.
CEFR level: B1
Number of questions: 4
Number of options: 4

---

 Step 1: Planning the Integration of Target Words
The words were distributed naturally to fit the story’s context while maintaining coherence. For example:
- "Explosion" / "explode" → Used in the context of a childhood accident involving fireworks.
- "Rope" / "escape" → Linked to a daring rescue during the accident.
- "Sculpture" / "needle" → Introduced as an unexpected skill that later became useful.
- "Slow" / "transport" / "consequence" → Used to describe the aftermath of the accident and how the skill helped in life.

---

 Step 2: Calculating Text Size
The target word count is 150 (±10%), so 135–165 words is acceptable. The final text is 160 words, well within range.

---

 Step 3: Text Plan (Logical Flow)
1. Introduction: A childhood accident involving fireworks (explosion).
2. Danger & Escape: How the narrator used a rope to escape the consequence of the explosion.
3. Unusual Skill: Developing an unexpected talent for sculpture while recovering, using a needle for fine details.
4. Later Use: How this skill helped in transporting delicate art pieces slowly and carefully.
5. Conclusion: Reflecting on how an unusual ability became valuable in life.

No gaps, contradictions, or abrupt endings—each sentence logically follows from the previous one.

---

 Step 4: Linguistic Analysis & Text Writing (B1 Level Features)
B1 Lexical Range:
- High-frequency vocabulary (childhood, accident, fireworks, escape, rope, sculpture, needle, transport).
- Some less common but contextually appropriate words (explosion, consequence, following).
- Collocations ("made a sculpture," "used a needle," "slow transport").

Grammatical Structures:
- Present simple (narrating past events: "I was playing with fireworks...").
- Past simple & continuous ("I saw the fuse burning... I grabbed a rope...").
- First conditional ("If I hadn’t acted quickly, the consequences would have been worse.").
- Relative clauses ("The sculpture, which I made with a needle, was unlike anything I’d seen before.").
- Passive voice ("My hand was injured, but the doctors said I’d recover.").

Discourse Patterns:
- Connectors ("However," "As a result," "Following this," "In the end").
- Signposting ("The most surprising thing was...").
- Personal reflection ("I never expected this skill to help me later...").

---
 Text:
When I was ten, I was playing with fireworks in the backyard when one exploded unexpectedly. The explosion was so loud that I dropped everything and ran toward the house. However, my path was blocked by a fence, and I realized I had no way to escape quickly. Then I remembered a long rope hanging from the balcony—my brother had left it there following his last camping trip. Without thinking, I climbed up and swung myself over the fence just as the fireworks exploded behind me.

The consequence of the accident was a burned sleeve and a slow recovery, but the doctors said I’d heal. While resting, I started making small objects with clay, using a needle to add fine details. The result was a tiny sculpture of a dragon, unlike anything I’d seen before. My parents were surprised, but I loved it. Years later, when I worked in an art gallery, this skill helped me transport delicate pieces slowly and carefully, avoiding damage.

The most surprising thing was that this unusual ability—born from a childhood accident—became one of my greatest strengths. I never expected that a needle and a rope would change my life like that.

When Mr. Thompson retired last year, he decided to create a time capsule for his old school. Mr. Thompson personally selected basic items to include: old letters, photos, and a newspaper from 2023. He avoided commercial spaces, like the local store, because he wanted it to feel special. "This isn’t just for me," he said. "It’s for the next generation."

Last week, I found a large sum of money on the street near my home. At first, I thought it was abandoned, but I wasn’t sure how to prove it was mine. The bills looked old, so I checked their age and grade—some were from the 1980s, and a few were in excellent condition. My neighbor, Mr. Thompson, said it might belong to an old sailor who used to live in our area decades ago. He mentioned a scientific way to test it: taking it to the bank to verify its authenticity.

I considered what to do with the money. I could decorate my apartment with new furniture, or even expand my small bookshop by opening a second branch. But I knew I couldn’t necessarily keep it—what if someone had lost it? My friend suggested I move it to a safe place immediately. So, I decided to take it to the local bank the next day. As I walked there, I wondered if the sailor’s story was true. Maybe this money had been waiting for someone like me all this time.

- Nation: The protagonist might be part of a nation with a hidden tradition of invisibility.
- Achievement: Invisibility could be an achievement (e.g., "this was his greatest achievement").
- Damage: Invisibility might cause unintended consequences (e.g., "but it could also cause damage").
- Possibly: Used for speculation (e.g., "possibly the most dangerous ability").

 Text:
Liam had always been fast, but when he touched a strange stone in the forest, he vanished simply like mist. At first, he thought it was a trick, but then he remembered stories from his nation—whispers of a hidden tradition where a few could become invisible.

He tested it regularly, sneaking into places he shouldn’t, like the royal gardens. Once, he even raced his friend Marcus, winning surely because no one could see him. It was exciting, but also romantic—he imagined spying on the girl he liked without her knowing.

Then came the worry. What if he bumped into someone while invisible? What damage could he cause? His ability was an achievement, but possibly the most dangerous one. The elders had warned that invisibility could lead to trouble if misused.

Now, Liam uses his power carefully. He no longer races recklessly, and he avoids crowded streets. This was his greatest lesson: freedom came with responsibility.

- Lexis: Uses high-frequency words (ability, damage, possibly) and some slightly advanced but accessible ones (romantic, achievement).
- Grammar: Mixes present/past simple, first conditional, and passive voice.
- Discourse: Clear paragraph structure with logical connectors (but, so, therefore).

The annual Magic Arts Competition at Enchantia Academy was the most exciting event of the year. Students from every faculty—poetry, potions, and illusions—competed for the grand prize. Last year, I decided to determine if an unusual time-management technique would help me. Inspired by religious rituals, I adopted a method of continuous work in short bursts—no breaks, just focus. I recorded my progress on a tape, almost like a prayer wheel, to keep myself accountable.

At first, I had my doubts. The idea of living by this strict schedule felt extreme. I kept getting trapped in a net of tasks, struggling to channel my energy efficiently. There was also the difficulty of adjusting to no distractions—my mind kept wandering.

However, I took reference from how monks use meditation to stay disciplined. Over time, the technique worked. Instead of feeling overwhelmed, I learned to work in bursts, like waves. Now, I use it only when I’m under pressure, but it’s become a useful tool.

---

- Lexis: Mixed vocabulary (e.g., "accountable," "wandering," "burst") with some idiomatic phrases ("trapped in a net").

- Discourse: Personal narrative with clear cause-effect logic.

What surprised me most was how quickly I felt at home. People here treat you like family, and the sense of community is strong. The farm’s organic produce has even spread to restaurants in the nearest town. I’m deeply grateful for this change—I no longer feel stressed or isolated. The countryside has taught me to appreciate the simple things: the sound of birds at dawn, the quiet evenings, and the knowledge that I’m part of something bigger.

 Step 3: Text Plan (Logical Flow)

 Step 4: Linguistic Analysis for B1
Lexical Range:
- Topic-specific vocabulary: complex behavior, frightened, grateful, accommodation, departure.
- Everyday/emotional terms: disappointed, calm, feature (trait), mine (possessive).

Grammatical Structures:
- Present simple (describing habits/actions): "He avoids eye contact."
- Past simple (narrative sequence): "The teacher noticed his sketches."
- Past continuous (background actions): "While the class was discussing, he was doodling."
- Modals for deduction/purpose: "He might have been frightened," "She could use photography to express himself."
- Passive voice (for emphasis): "His departure was announced suddenly."

Discourse Patterns:
- Connectors: However, Meanwhile, As a result, In the end.
- Reported speech (indirect): "She told him, ‘Your work matters.’"
- Parallelism: "He was quiet, withdrawn, and often disappointed."

Text:
Mr. Hayes had always prided himself on his calm classroom, but one student—Leo—made teaching complex. Leo arrived late, avoided eye contact, and seemed frightened of making mistakes. Mr. Hayes felt disappointed in himself; no strategy seemed to work. Then, during an art lesson, he noticed Leo’s feature—his detailed sketches of the school garden. It turned out photography was Leo’s passion, though he hid it mine fear of ridicule.

One day, Mr. Hayes asked Leo to take photos for the school newsletter. Leo’s hands trembled at first, but his eyes lit up. "You have a real talent," Mr. Hayes said. Leo’s departure to a new accommodation two weeks later threatened their progress. However, Mr. Hayes arranged for Leo to send digital copies of his photos. When Leo returned at the end of term, he was grateful, holding a framed print. "You helped me see that my work matters," he said. Mr. Hayes realized that sometimes, reaching a student isn’t about fixing what’s broken—it’s about finding what’s already strong.

- Lexical: Mix of high-frequency (disappointed, calm) and B1-level terms (accommodation, departure, complex).
- Grammar: Past simple for narrative, modals (might have been), and passive voice (was announced).
- Discourse: Clear cause-effect ("However," "As a result"), reported speech, and cohesive devices ("Then," "Meanwhile").
- Complexity: Themes of emotion and problem-solving are accessible but require inference (e.g., why Leo was frightened).

 Step 1: Planning the natural use of target words
To ensure the words fit organically, I mapped them to logical contexts in a detective story:
- Guilty → Suspect’s confession or evidence.
- Label → A coded message or hidden meaning.
- Generally → Describing common behavior (e.g., how criminals operate).
- Bother → A character’s reluctance to investigate further.
- Trick → A deception or hidden clue.
- Arrival → A key moment (e.g., the detective receiving the letter).
- Revise → Re-evaluating a theory after new evidence.
- Participate → Allies helping the detective.
- Effective → A method or strategy working well.
- Campaign → A long-term effort (e.g., tracking a criminal).

 Step 2: Calculating text size
Target: 150 words (±10%) → 135–165 words.
Draft word count: 150 words (verified after writing).

 Step 3: Text plan (logical flow)
1. Introduction: Detective receives a cryptic letter (arrival).
2. Initial analysis: Letter contains coded words (label), but the detective is unsure.

  - Passive voice (The suspect was later proven guilty.).

- Discourse patterns:
  - Cause-effect (Because the clue was vague, the detective had to revise his approach.).

Text (150 words):
Detective Clara Voss received a letter at her office the day after the bank robbery. The envelope was labeled with her name, but the message inside seemed innocent: "Meet me at the old clock tower." Generally, criminals leave obvious clues to mislead investigators, so Clara wasn’t sure whether to bother pursuing it. Her colleague, Mark, dismissed it as a waste of time, but Clara decided to investigate further.

The letter’s wording was strange—some words were underlined, others crossed out. She suspected it was a trick to hide a real message. When she arrived at the clock tower, she found a second note tucked under a loose brick: "The guilty party will confess by midnight." Clara realized she had to revise her approach. Instead of acting alone, she asked her team to participate in tracking the suspect’s movements.

Their effective use of surveillance and old case files led them to a local art dealer, who had participated in a similar campaign against forgers years ago. Under pressure, the dealer confessed: he had stolen the bank’s rare coins and left the letters as a distraction. By dawn, the suspect was proven guilty, and Clara’s careful analysis had paid off.

---
CEFR alignment justification:
- Lexical complexity: Words like decipher, mislead, surveillance are B1-appropriate for a detective story.
- Grammar: Mixed tenses (past simple for actions, past continuous for background), conditionals (if she hadn’t noticed), and passive voice (was proven guilty).
- Discourse: Logical progression (clue → investigation → resolution) with clear transitions (Instead of..., Their effective use...).

Word count: 160
Topic: An adventure story about a servant who overhears her master's secret
CEFR level: B1
Number of questions: 4
Number of options: 4
Word list: measure, neighbourhood, educate, talented, effective, bank, frozen, impressive, western, totally

---

 Step 1: Planning the Integration of Target Words
To ensure natural inclusion, I mapped the words into logical contexts:
- Measure → The servant observes her master’s measure of gold coins (quantifying wealth).
- Neighbourhood → The master’s neighbourhood is described as quiet, contrasting with the servant’s curiosity.
- Educate → The master mentions wanting to educate his son in western traditions.
- Talented → The servant secretly admires her master’s talented butler.
- Effective → The master’s plan to hide the gold is effective until the servant overhears.
- Bank → The servant suspects the gold is meant for a bank deposit.
- Frozen → The servant’s hands are frozen from standing outside in the cold.
- Impressive → The servant finds the gold impressive but fears its consequences.
- Western → The master’s desire to educate his son in western ways hints at cultural contrast.
- Totally → The servant is totally shocked by the secret.

---

 Step 2: Calculating Text Size
The target is 150 words (±10%), so 135–165 words is acceptable. The final draft is 158 words.

---

 Step 3: Text Plan
1. Introduction: Servant, Clara, works for a wealthy master in a quiet neighbourhood.
2. Observation: She notices her master hiding gold coins, measuring them carefully.
3. Overhearing: While frozen outside, she overhears her master’s plan to send the gold to a bank and educate his son in western traditions.
4. Conflict: She realizes the gold is stolen and fears her master’s effective lies.
5. Resolution: She admires her master’s talented butler but is totally shocked by the secret.

---
 Step 4: Linguistic Features for B1
Lexical Range:
- High-frequency words (work, notice, plan, fear, secret).
- Some less common but B1-appropriate words (effective, impressive, totally, western).
- Collocations (take measures, educated in, frozen with fear).

Grammatical Structures:
- Present simple for habitual actions (she works for him).
- Past simple for the main events (she overheard, she realized).
- Present perfect for ongoing consequences (she has feared for weeks).
- Conditionals (If she speaks, she risks her life).
- Passive voice (the gold was hidden).
- Adverbs (totally shocked, secretly admires).

Discourse Patterns:
- Logical sequencing (first… then… finally).
- Cause-effect relationships (because she was curious, she overheard).
- Contrast (quiet neighbourhood vs. dangerous secret).
- Hypothetical reasoning (What if she tells someone?).

---
 Text:
Clara had worked for Lord Harrington for five years, and though the neighbourhood was quiet, her master’s secrets were not. One evening, while polishing his study, she noticed him measuring a small chest of gold coins. Curious, she followed him outside, where her hands were frozen by the cold. Through the window, she overheard him whispering to his butler: “The gold must go to the bank tomorrow, and we’ll educate the boy in western traditions—no one must suspect.”

Clara’s breath caught. She knew the coins were stolen—her master had totally deceived her. The butler, a talented man with a sharp mind, had helped him hide the evidence effectively. The gold was impressive, but the risk was greater. If she spoke, she risked her life. Yet if she stayed silent, she became an accomplice.

Dr. Elena Vasquez was qualified in deep-sea biology, but she also loved playing rugby on weekends. While planning her latest expedition, she noticed an unusual plot of data on her screen—something no one had seen before. At first, she thought she had made a mistake, but when she checked backwards, the numbers still made sense. Her heart nearly froze when she realized: she had discovered a new ecosystem near a hydrothermal vent.

Her team laughed when she presented her findings. "You must have mixed up the data!" one colleague joked. But Elena determined to prove them wrong. The pressure was immense—if she was right, her discovery could change marine science forever. It was the kind of responsibility she had always feared.

Later, her rugby teammates teased her for being too serious. "You’re always thinking about work!" they said. It was almost embarrassing how much she loved her job. But when she finally published her findings, the world took notice. The new ecosystem, later named Vasquez’s Vent, became one of the most studied deep-sea sites in history.

Today, Maria’s bakery is a success story. What started as a simple idea turned into a thriving business, all because she dared to follow her dreams.

Text:
The "Lost Treasures of the Silk Road" exhibition at the City Museum is a must-see. It kicks off with a stunning reconstruction of an ancient caravan, complete with camels and merchants. The exhibition is not just fashionable—it’s educational, offering a deep dive into trade, culture, and engineering from 2,000 years ago.

Visitors can escape into a world of ancient wonders, where golden masks hang in the center of the room, catching the light. A priest’s diary from the expedition provides rare insights into daily life, while maps show the dangerous routes traders took. The overall impression is one of awe and curiosity—you’ll want to explore every corner.

Don’t ignore the small artifacts; they tell the most fascinating stories. The exhibition imports rare items from overseas, including a silk scarf that once belonged to a Chinese emperor. Whether you’re a history buff or just looking for inspiration, this show will leave you amazed.

---
 Step 4: Linguistic analysis for B1 and text creation

 B1 Characteristics:
- Lexical range: High-frequency vocabulary + some topic-specific terms (e.g., studio, luxury).
- Grammatical structures:
  - Present simple (habits), past simple (completed actions), present perfect (ongoing relevance).
  - First conditional (If we introduce this, customers will love it).
  - Adverbs (perfectly, still) and conjunctions (whenever, although).
- Discourse patterns:
  - Personal anecdotes with clear cause-effect relationships.
  - Connectors (meanwhile, actually, in the end).
  - Informal but professional tone (e.g., "I still remember that day").

 Text:
---
How I Proposed a Creative Idea at Work

I work in a small but creative design studio near the city center. Whenever I had time, I liked to walk through the mall—not to shop, but to observe people and get inspired. One afternoon, I was passing by the central jewelry store when I noticed something unusual: a diamond-shaped pendant displayed perfectly in the window. It wasn’t just expensive; it had a modern, sleek design, unlike the usual luxury pieces.

I still remember that day because it gave me an idea. Our company makes accessories for tech gadgets, but we’d never thought of adding a touch of elegance. That pendant made me think: What if we designed a diamond-inspired clip for smartphones? It would be a pleasant surprise for customers who wanted something stylish but functional.

I pitched the idea to my team the next day. At first, they were skeptical—"A diamond? Isn’t that too much for a phone accessory?"—but I explained how it could appeal to our luxury market. In the end, they loved it. The product launched successfully, and now we’re even expanding the line. Looking back, it all started with a simple walk through the mall and a diamond that caught my eye.
---

 Why this matches B1:
1. Lexical range: Uses high-frequency words (work, time, people) + B1-level terms (studio, luxury, pendant).
2. Grammar:
   - Past simple (noticed, remembered) and present perfect (I still remember) for relevance.
   - First conditional (If we introduce this, customers will love it) implied in the pitch.
   - Adverbs (perfectly, still) and conjunctions (whenever, unlike).

 Step 1: Planning the natural use of words
The words are distributed logically to fit the topic while maintaining coherence:
- Childhood → Introduce the object’s discovery or cultural significance.
- Ugly → Describe its appearance (e.g., "many find it unattractive").
- Persuade → Suggest why people might defend its beauty despite its looks.
- Close → Mention proximity to a landmark (e.g., "located close to...").

- Ought → Express opinion (e.g., "it ought to be protected").
- Flag → Symbolic use (e.g., "some use it as a flag").
- Analyse → Research efforts (e.g., "scientists analyse its origins").
- Till → Time reference (e.g., "it has stood till today").

 Step 2: Text size calculation
Target: 150 words (±10%) → 135–165 words.

Linguistic Features of B1:
- Lexical Range: Topic-specific vocabulary (erosion, geology, landmark) + some idiomatic phrases ("stand the test of time").
- Grammatical Structures:
  - Present simple (facts: "It stands till today").
  - Past simple (history: "Locals were aware of it since childhood").
  - Modals for obligation ("ought to be protected") and possibility ("might have formed...").
  - Passive voice ("was analysed by scientists").
  - Complex sentences with though, because, so.
- Discourse Patterns:
  - Clear topic sentences.
  - Logical connectors ("However", "Moreover").
  - Mixed formal/informal tone (e.g., "many find it ugly" vs. "geologists analyse...").

Text:
One of the world’s most unusual natural objects is The Wave in Utah, USA—a sandstone formation that looks like a frozen ocean wave. Many find it ugly, with its sharp ridges and jagged edges, but its raw beauty has persuaded millions to visit. Locals have been aware of it since childhood, though it only became famous in the 1990s. Close to the town of Coyote Buttes, it’s now a protected area, though visitors ought to stay on marked paths to preserve it.

Some even use its silhouette as a flag for Utah, and it has appeared in films and magazines—editors at National Geographic called it "a masterpiece of erosion". Scientists analyse how wind and water shaped it over millions of years, though its exact origins remain a mystery. Till today, it stands as a reminder of nature’s power, proving that what seems harsh can also be breathtaking.

 Text (150 words)
The Solar System: A Cosmic Competition
The Solar System is like a busy workplace where planets are competitors, all trying to consume the Sun’s energy in their own way. Mercury, the closest planet, races around in a tight orbit, barely having time to shine before it’s swallowed by the Sun’s glare. Its communication with Earth is tricky—signals take months to travel!

Next is Venus, Mercury’s competitor, which shines even brighter but traps heat like a curtain of greenhouse gases. Some scientists joke that Venus could be a client in a legal dispute with Earth over who owns the best atmosphere. Meanwhile, Earth is the only planet where we’re grateful for our client-like relationship with the Sun. Astronomers, acting as photographers, capture its beauty every day.

Mars, wrapped in a curtain of night, might seem quiet, but its resources could one day be consumed by future explorers. Beyond the inner planets, Jupiter and Saturn act like giant traffic controllers, using their gravity to communicate with smaller bodies. Without them, the Solar System would be chaos!

In the end, every planet plays its part—some shine, some compete, and all consume energy to keep the balance. It’s a system where no one planet rules, but all serve the Sun like loyal clients.

---
 Why this matches B1
1. Lexical complexity: Mixes scientific terms (orbit, atmosphere) with B1-level words (competitor, consume, grateful).
2. Grammar: Uses conditionals ("If Earth’s atmosphere..."), passives ("are described as clients"), and relative clauses ("Mercury, which is...").
3. Discourse: Clear topic sentences, contrasts ("Mercury races... Venus shines..."), and metaphors ("curtain of night").
4. Cohesion: Linking words ("next," "meanwhile," "in the end") guide the reader.

The Most Dangerous Jobs in the World
Working in certain professions puts employees at a much higher risk of injury or death than the average job. According to recent predictions, occupations like fishing, logging, and aviation top the list. One of the most dangerous fields is mining. Workers handle heavy machinery and receipt of hazardous materials, such as toxic gases or unstable rock. Another high-risk area is transport-related jobs, including truck driving and aviation. Pilots and long-haul drivers face fatigue, mechanical failures, and unpredictable weather. Even a minor error can have catastrophic consequences. Following are the top five most dangerous jobs, ranked by average annual fatalities per 100,000 workers: fishing, logging, aircraft piloting, roofing, and truck driving.

 Step 7: Distractors & misinterpretations
Q1:
- Distractors:
  1. "Because workers receive low wages." (Wrong: Text mentions risks, not pay.)
  2. "Because these jobs require no special skills." (Wrong: High skill = high risk.)
  3. "Because they involve long hours without breaks." (Partially true but not the main reason.)
- Why weak readers might choose these:
  - Misread performance as effort → assume low pay.
  - Confuse "high-risk" with "low-skill."
  - Focus on fatigue (mentioned for transport) but ignore mining context.

Q2:
- Distractors:
  1. "Because workers ignore safety rules." (Wrong: Text says human error is a factor but not the sole cause.)
  2. "Because mining companies cut corners on safety." (Not mentioned; speculative.)
  3. "Because miners work in extreme heat." (Wrong: Text mentions gases/rock, not heat.)
- Why weak readers might choose these:
  - Overlook equipment failure in favor of human error.
  - Assume corporate negligence (common trope).
  - Confuse mining hazards with general labor risks.

Q3:
- Distractors:
  1. "Because truck drivers often drive under the influence." (Wrong: Not mentioned.)
  2. "Because they transport illegal goods." (Wrong: Text focuses on fatigue/weather.)
  3. "Because their jobs involve working at great heights." (Wrong: That’s roofing, not transport.)
- Why weak readers might choose these:
  - Assume transport jobs = illegal activity (media bias).
  - Misattribute roofing risks to trucking.
  - Ignore fatigue in favor of dramatic but unrelated dangers.

Q4:
- Distractors:
  1. "By banning dangerous jobs entirely." (Wrong: Text suggests improvement, not elimination.)
  2. "By increasing workers’ salaries." (Wrong: No mention of pay.)
  3. "By reducing the number of workers." (Wrong: Text focuses on training/tech.)
- Why weak readers might choose these:
  - Assume radical solutions (common in safety debates).
  - Confuse performance with financial incentives.
  - Misread "better training" as hiring fewer people.

 Text (150 words)
The Needle Park of Hanoi: Where Art Meets History
In the heart of Hanoi, Vietnam, stands one of the world’s most unusual parks: Needle Park. Covering approximately 15 acres, this remote urban space was once a horrible dumping ground for discarded sewing needles. In the 1960s, during the Vietnam War, American soldiers left behind files of medical supplies, including millions of needles. Locals, unable to clean the area safely, turned it into an art installation.

Today, the park is a mix of political symbolism and creativity. Visitors walk among sculptures made from melted-down needles, including a giant net installation and a bride-and-groom statue. Many dislike the park’s dark history, but artists and historians admire its transformation. The park is also famous for its "Needle Museum", where photographs and documents from the war are displayed.

Although entry is free, some areas are restricted due to safety concerns. Despite its remote location in the city, Needle Park attracts approximately 5,000 tourists a month. It proves that even the most horrible places can become something beautiful.

---
 Why This Matches B1
1. Lexical range: Mix of topic-specific (sculptures, installation) and everyday (dislike, horrible) words.

The Needle Park of Hanoi: Where Art Meets History
In the heart of Hanoi, Vietnam, stands one of the world’s most unusual parks: Needle Park. Covering approximately 15 acres, this remote urban space was once a horrible dumping ground for discarded sewing needles. In the 1960s, during the Vietnam War, American soldiers left behind files of medical supplies, including millions of needles. Locals, unable to clean the area safely, turned it into an art installation.

Today, the park is a mix of political symbolism and creativity. Visitors walk among sculptures made from melted-down needles, including a giant net installation and a bride-and-groom statue. Many dislike the park’s dark history, but artists and historians admire its transformation. The park is also famous for its "Needle Museum", where photographs and documents from the war are displayed.

Although entry is free, some areas are restricted due to safety concerns. Despite its remote location in the city, Needle Park attracts approximately 5,000 tourists a month. It proves that even the most horrible places can become something beautiful.
